questions.question: In which year did Carl Anderson discover a positively charged particle called 'positron' whose mass appears to be equal to the mass of an electron?
questions.questionHtml: In which year did Carl Anderson discover a positively charged particle called 'positron' whose mass appears to be equal to the mass of an electron?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is 1932.

Key Points

  • Carl Anderson:-
    • He was an American physicist who won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1936 for his discovery of the positron.
    • Anderson's discovery also led to the development of positron emission tomography (PET), which is now widely used in medical imaging.

Additional Information

  • Positron:-
    • It is the antiparticle of an electron and has the same mass as that of an electron but carries a positive charge.
    • The discovery of the positron provided evidence for the existence of antimatter, which was predicted by Paul Dirac in 1928.

questions.question: What is the starting voltage of an AA battery used for home gadgets such as remote controls, small toys, and wireless kitchen appliances?
questions.questionHtml: What is the starting voltage of an AA battery used for home gadgets such as remote controls, small toys, and wireless kitchen appliances?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is 1.5 V.

Key Points

  • AA batteries measure at 1.5V and work well for devices that require a somewhat high current draw but are not in constant use.
  • For example, an alkaline battery, like a AA or AAA, has a nominal voltage of about 1.5V, while the voltage of a LiPo battery will normally be around 3.7V. The key word here is 'nominal', as the actual voltage of the battery will fluctuate turn on how much charge it has left.
  •  A classic nominal voltage, most AA, AAA, C, & D cells are 1.5 volts, and many household and handheld devices have been built to use that voltage.
  • The first zinc-carbon dry cells naturally produced 1.5 volts of energy and have remained the standard ever since.

Additional Information

  • ​ An electric battery is a source of electric power consisting of one or more electrochemical cells with external connections for powering electrical devices. 
  • When a battery is supplying power, its positive terminal is the cathode and its negative terminal is the anode. 
  • The terminal marked negative is the source of electrons that will flow through an external electric circuit to the positive terminal.

B) As per Gay Lussac's law, at constant volume, pressure of a fixed amount of a gas varies directly with the temperature. C) Silicon is present in group 14 and period 3 of the periodic table.
questions.questionHtml:
Consider the following statements:

A) A gas that follows Boyle's law, Charles' law and Avogadro law is called an ideal gas.

B) As per Gay Lussac's law, at constant volume, pressure of a fixed amount of a gas varies directly with the temperature.

C) Silicon is present in group 14 and period 3 of the periodic table.

options.text: Both A and C is true
options.html: Both A and C is true

options.text: Both A and B is true
options.html: Both A and B is true

options.text: Only B and C is true
options.html: Only B and C is true

questions.solution: All three given statements (A, B, and C) are correct. An ideal gas follows Boyle's law, Charles' law, and Avogadro's law. According to Gay-Lussac's law, at constant volume, the pressure of a fixed amount of gas varies directly with the temperature in Kelvin. Silicon is correctly identified as being in group 14 and period 3 of the periodic table. Therefore, the correct option in the provided CSV data is option 4, which states that A, B, and C are true.

questions.question: In 1808, whose work provided a physical picture of how compounds are formed by the combination of two or more different types of atoms?
questions.questionHtml: In 1808, whose work provided a physical picture of how compounds are formed by the combination of two or more different types of atoms?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is John Dalton.
Key Points 
  • John Dalton was an English chemist, physicist, and meteorologist who is best known for his pioneering work in the development of modern atomic theory.
  • Dalton's atomic theory, which he proposed in 1808, provided a physical picture of how compounds are formed by the combination of two or more different types of atoms.
  • He suggested that all matter is made up of tiny, indivisible particles called atoms, which combine in fixed ratios to form compounds.
  • His theory was based on several key principles, including the idea that atoms of different elements have different weights and properties, that atoms can combine to form molecules, and that chemical reactions involve the rearrangement of atoms.
  • Dalton's work on atomic theory was groundbreaking and laid the foundation for modern chemistry.
  • He was also the first scientist to study the behavior of gases and to develop a method for measuring the relative weights of atoms.
Additional Information

George Zweig

  • He proposed the concept of quarks in 1964, which are subatomic particles that makeup protons and neutrons.
  • He suggested that quarks come in six different "flavors" and that they are held together by a strong nuclear force.
  • Joseph J Thomson
  • He discovered the electron in 1897 while studying cathode rays.
  • He proposed the plum pudding model of the atom, which suggested that atoms were made up of a positively charged substance with negatively charged electrons embedded in it.

Niels Bohr

  • He developed the Bohr model of the atom in 1913, which proposed that electrons orbit the nucleus at fixed energy levels.
  • He also suggested that electrons can jump between energy levels by absorbing or emitting energy in the form of photons.

questions.question: For a chemical reaction with rise in temperature by 10°, the rate constant becomes nearly ________________.
questions.questionHtml: For a chemical reaction with rise in temperature by 10°, the rate constant becomes nearly ________________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Double.

Key Points

  • For many chemical reactions, the rate constant approximately doubles with a 10°C increase in temperature.
  • This phenomenon is often referred to as the "rule of thumb" in chemical kinetics.
  • The temperature dependence of the rate constant is described by the Arrhenius equation.
  • According to the Arrhenius equation, the rate constant (k) is related to temperature (T) through the exponential factor involving activation energy (Ea) and the gas constant (R).

Additional Information

  • Arrhenius Equation:
    • The Arrhenius equation is k = A * exp(-Ea/(RT)), where k is the rate constant, A is the pre-exponential factor (frequency of collisions), Ea is the activation energy, R is the gas constant, and T is the temperature in Kelvin.
    • This equation shows the relationship between the rate constant and temperature, indicating that as temperature increases, the rate constant increases exponentially.
  • Activation Energy (Ea):
    • Activation energy is the minimum energy that reacting molecules must possess to undergo a chemical reaction.
    • Higher activation energy means that fewer molecules have sufficient energy to react at a given temperature.
  • Gas Constant (R):
    • The gas constant (R) is a physical constant that appears in many fundamental equations in physical sciences, such as the ideal gas law and the Arrhenius equation.
    • The value of R is 8.314 J/(mol·K).
  • Rule of Thumb in Chemical Kinetics:
    • The "rule of thumb" in chemical kinetics suggests that for many reactions, the rate constant approximately doubles for every 10°C rise in temperature.
    • This empirical rule helps chemists estimate the effect of temperature changes on reaction rates without detailed calculations.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most acidic?
questions.questionHtml: Which of the following is the most acidic?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is HCOOH.

Key Points

  • HCOOH, also known as formic acid, is the simplest carboxylic acid and is the most acidic among the given options.
  • Formic acid has the highest acidity due to the absence of electron-donating alkyl groups which decrease the acidity by destabilizing the conjugate base.
  • The other options, such as C2H5COOH (propanoic acid), C3H7COOH (butanoic acid), and CH3COOH (acetic acid), have alkyl groups that reduce their acidity.
  • Formic acid is widely used in various industrial processes and has a higher acid dissociation constant (Ka) compared to other carboxylic acids listed.

Additional Information

  • Carboxylic Acids
    • Carboxylic acids are organic acids characterized by the presence of a carboxyl group (–COOH).
    • The acidity of carboxylic acids is due to the resonance stabilization of the carboxylate anion (R-COO−) formed after deprotonation.
    • Electron-withdrawing groups increase acidity by stabilizing the carboxylate anion, while electron-donating groups decrease acidity by destabilizing it.
  • Acid Dissociation Constant (Ka)
    • The acid dissociation constant (Ka) is a quantitative measure of the strength of an acid in solution.
    • It is the equilibrium constant for the dissociation of an acid into its conjugate base and a proton (H+).
    • Higher Ka values indicate stronger acids, as they dissociate more completely in solution.
    • Formic acid has a higher Ka value compared to the other carboxylic acids listed, making it more acidic.
  • Factors Influencing Acidity
    • Inductive Effect: Electron-withdrawing groups increase acidity, while electron-donating groups decrease it.
    • Resonance Effect: Resonance stabilization of the conjugate base increases acidity.
    • Hybridization: Acidity increases with the s-character of the hybrid orbital holding the acidic hydrogen (sp > sp2 > sp3).
    • Solvation: Better solvation of the conjugate base in a solvent increases acidity.

questions.question: Which of the following techniques can be used to separate the impurities in Milk?
questions.questionHtml: Which of the following techniques can be used to separate the impurities in Milk?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Column chromatography.

Key Points

  • Column Chromatography
    • The separation and purification of substances from a solution to obtain the simpler substances from the complex elements is called column chromatography.
    • The process of separation employs five different types of column chromatography.
    • The two phases of the procedure are the mobile phase and the stationary phase.  
    •  In this solid-liquid method, the stationary phase is a solid and the mobile phase is a liquid or gas.
    • Applications of Column Chromatography
      • separation of a complex mixture.
      • purification or the process of removing impurities.
      • isolation of the active elements.
      • removing metabolites from bodily fluids.
      • estimation of pharmaceutical compounds or crude extracts.
      • Column Chromatography can also be used to separate the impurities in Milk.

Additional Information

  • Microscopy
    • The method of viewing things that are invisible to the naked eye is called microscopy.
    • ​The range can be any value between mm and nm.
    • Optical microscopy, scanning probe microscopy, and electron microscopy are the three main microscopic techniques that are used.
  • Microtomy
    • Microtomy is a technique that can be used instead of electropolishing and ion milling to prepare thin sections for materials like bones, minerals, and teeth.
    • The section thickness of a microtome can be adjusted to be between 50 nm and 100 m, thin enough to divide a human hair across its breadth.
  • Autoclave
    • An autoclave is a device used to perform industrial and scientific procedures that demand for higher pressure and/or temperature than ambient conditions.
    • To eliminate dangerous germs, viruses, fungus, and spores on objects inside a pressure vessel, steam is used under pressure in this machine.

questions.question: Identify an example of plasma as a state of matter.
questions.questionHtml: Identify an example of plasma as a state of matter.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Neon sign bulbs.

Key Points

  • Neon sign bulbs are an excellent example of plasma as a state of matter.
  • Plasma is created in neon sign bulbs when an electric current passes through the gas, ionizing it and creating plasma.
  • The plasma in neon sign bulbs emits light, which is characteristic of neon signs.
  • Plasma is the fourth state of matter, distinct from solid, liquid, and gas, and is created under high-energy conditions.

Additional Information

  • Plasma
    • Plasma is known as the fourth state of matter, consisting of a collection of free-moving ions and electrons.
    • It is formed at very high temperatures when gases are ionized.
    • Examples of plasma include the Sun, stars, lightning, and neon signs.
    • Plasma is distinct from the other states of matter due to its unique properties such as electrical conductivity, magnetic fields, and the ability to emit light.
  • Neon
    • Neon is a noble gas that is colorless, odorless, and inert under standard conditions.
    • It is used in neon signs where it emits a bright orange-red light when electrified.
    • Neon signs work by passing an electric current through the neon gas, which ionizes the atoms and creates plasma.
  • Ionization
    • Ionization is the process by which an atom or molecule gains or loses electrons, forming ions.
    • This process is fundamental in the formation of plasma.
    • Ionization can occur through various means such as heating, electric fields, or radiation.

options.html: Elements react to form new compounds.

questions.solution:
The incorrect statement is Compounds have a variable composition.

  • Compounds have a fixed composition throughout the mass, Hence Option 2 is Not true.

 Key Points

  • Properties of Compound
    • A compound is a substance made up of two or more elements chemically combined in a fixed proportion by mass.
    • A compound cannot be separated into its constituents by physical processes (It can only be separated into
      its constituents by chemical processes).
    • The properties of a compound are entirely different from those of its constituents.
    • Energy (in the form of heat, light, etc.) is usually given out or absorbed during the preparation of a compound.
    • The composition of a compound is fixed, the constituents are present in a fixed proportion by mass.
    • A compound has a definite formula.
    • A compound has a fixed melting point, boiling point.

questions.question: The type of reaction that is typically found when a material that is required for the reaction to proceed, such as a surface or a catalyst, is saturated by the reactants is called a ________ order reaction.
questions.questionHtml: The type of reaction that is typically found when a material that is required for the reaction to proceed, such as a surface or a catalyst, is saturated by the reactants is called a ________ order reaction.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is zero order reaction.

Key Points

  • In a zero-order reaction, the rate of reaction is independent of the concentration of the reactants.
  • These reactions are commonly seen in catalytic processes where the catalyst surface is saturated by the reactants.
  • In such reactions, the rate of reaction remains constant until the reactant concentration is significantly depleted.
  • Zero-order kinetics is often observed in heterogeneous catalysis and other situations where a limiting step is saturated.

Additional Information

  • First-order Reaction
    • A first-order reaction is one where the rate is directly proportional to the concentration of one reactant.
    • The rate law for a first-order reaction can be expressed as: Rate = k[A], where k is the rate constant and [A] is the concentration of the reactant.
    • These reactions often involve unimolecular processes.
    • Examples include radioactive decay and certain substitution reactions in organic chemistry.
  • Second-order Reaction
    • A second-order reaction's rate is proportional to the square of the concentration of one reactant or the product of the concentrations of two reactants.
    • The rate law can be written as: Rate = k[A]^2 or Rate = k[A][B], depending on the reaction mechanism.
    • These reactions often involve bimolecular processes.
    • Examples include the reaction between hydrogen and iodine to form hydrogen iodide.
  • Third-order Reaction
    • A third-order reaction's rate depends on the concentration of three reactants or the concentration of one reactant raised to the third power, or other combinations summing to three.
    • The rate law can be expressed as: Rate = k[A]^3 or other combinations.
    • These reactions are less common compared to first and second-order reactions.
    • An example is the reaction between nitric oxide and oxygen to form nitrogen dioxide.

questions.question: It has been proved that, during a chemical reaction, atoms are neither created nor destroyed. This law is also known as the:
questions.questionHtml: It has been proved that, during a chemical reaction, atoms are neither created nor destroyed. This law is also known as the:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is law of conservation of mass.

Key Points

  • According to the law of conservation of mass, The matter can be neither created nor destroyed.
  • In other words, the mass of an object or collection of objects never changes, no matter how the parts are rearranged.
  • In an ordinary chemical reaction, the sum of the masses of the reactants (the substances undergoing the change) equals the sum of the masses of the products (the substances formed during the process).

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a neutral oxide?
questions.questionHtml: Which of the following is NOT a neutral oxide?
questions.solution: Sodium Oxide (Na<sub>2</sub>O) is not a neutral oxide because it is a metal oxide and reacts with water to form a strong base (NaOH). Neutral oxides do not react in the presence of any acid or base and are chemically stable.

questions.question: Which of the following acids is responsible for the sharp flavour in soft drinks?

questions.question: Which among the following alloys is a combination of gold and silver?
questions.questionHtml: Which among the following alloys is a combination of gold and silver?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Electrum.
Key Points
  • Electrum is a naturally occurring alloy of gold and silver, with trace amounts of other metals.
  • A naturally occurring alloy of silver and gold, electrum also contains trace amounts of copper and other metals.
  • Depending on the ratio of gold to silver, the color can range from light yellow to brilliant yellow. It's also called "green gold" and was created artificially.
  • As far back as the third millennium BC, electrum was utilized in the Old Kingdom of Egypt. It was occasionally applied as an outer layer to the pyramidions that topped Egyptian pyramids and obelisks.

Additional Information

  • Bronze is an alloy of copper and tin, sometimes with the addition of other metals. It is commonly used in sculpture, tools, and weapons.
  • Constantan is an alloy of copper and nickel, with a low temperature coefficient of resistance. It is commonly used in electrical and electronic applications.
  • Solder is a metal alloy used to join two pieces of metal together by melting it and allowing it to cool and solidify. It typically contains lead, tin, and other metals.

questions.question: The process of depositing a layer of any desired metal on another material by means of electricity is called ____________.
questions.questionHtml: The process of depositing a layer of any desired metal on another material by means of electricity is called ____________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is electroplating.

Key Points

  • Electroplating is a process used to coat the surface of a metal with a thin layer of another metal using an electric current.
  • It is commonly used for decorative purposes, corrosion protection, and to improve wear resistance.
  • The process involves immersing both the item to be plated and the plating metal in an electrolyte solution and applying a current.
  • The plating metal acts as the anode, and the item to be plated acts as the cathode, causing metal ions to move and deposit on the item.
  • Materials commonly used for electroplating include gold, silver, nickel, and chromium.

Additional Information

  • Electrolysis:
    • Electrolysis is a broader term that refers to the decomposition of a substance by passing an electric current through it.
    • It is used in various applications, including electroplating, electrorefining, and electrolysis of water to produce hydrogen and oxygen.
  • Anode and Cathode:
    • In electroplating, the anode is the metal that will be deposited, and the cathode is the item that is being plated.
    • The anode is positively charged, while the cathode is negatively charged.
  • Electrolyte Solution:
    • The electrolyte solution is a liquid that contains ions and conducts electricity, facilitating the movement of metal ions from the anode to the cathode.
    • Common electrolytes include solutions of metal salts, such as copper sulfate for copper plating.
  • Applications of Electroplating:
    • Electroplating is used in various industries, including automotive, jewelry, electronics, and aerospace.
    • It enhances the appearance, durability, and conductivity of the plated items.

questions.question: Which of the following organic compounds is a benzenoid?
questions.questionHtml: Which of the following organic compounds is a benzenoid?
questions.solution: Aniline is a benzenoid compound due to the presence of a benzene ring in its structure. Benzenoid compounds are aromatic and must contain at least one benzene ring. Aniline, with the chemical formula C6H5NH2, is an aromatic amine, important in the production of dyes, drugs, and plastics. Other compounds listed, such as acetaldehyde, propane, and hexane, lack a benzene ring and are not benzenoid. Aromatic compounds adhere to Hückel's rule, requiring a planar ring of overlapping p-orbitals and 4n+2 π-electrons. Aniline is industrially synthesized by reducing nitrobenzene or aminating chlorobenzene and undergoes electrophilic substitution reactions.

questions.question: In 1960, which isotope was used to define the standard measure of length?
questions.questionHtml: In 1960, which isotope was used to define the standard measure of length?
questions.solution: Krypton-86 was used in 1960 to define the meter based on the wavelength of its emitted radiation, as adopted by the 11th General Conference on Weights and Measures (CGPM). This provided a more precise standard than previous methods. In 1983, the definition changed to the distance light travels in a vacuum in 1/299,792,458 seconds, linking the meter to the fundamental constant, the speed of light. This redefinition aimed to enhance the precision and universality of the meter. The CGPM is the international authority ensuring uniformity in measurements.

questions.question: Calculate the oxidation number of 'S' in H 2 S 2 O 7 .
questions.questionHtml: Calculate the oxidation number of 'S' in H<sub>2</sub>S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>.
questions.solution: To determine the oxidation number of sulfur (S) in H₂S₂O₇, follow these key points: 1. Denote the oxidation number of sulfur as 'x'. 2. Assign oxidation numbers: Hydrogen (H) is +1 and Oxygen (O) is -2. 3. Set up the equation based on the molecule's overall charge (0): 2(+1) + 2(x) + 7(-2) = 0. 4. Simplify the equation: 2 + 2x - 14 = 0, leading to 2x = 12, thus x = +6. 5. Therefore, the oxidation number of sulfur in H₂S₂O₇ is +6.

questions.question: When you take Lead nitrate powder in a boiling tube and heat it, you will observe the emission of brown fumes that are of _________________.
questions.questionHtml: When you take Lead nitrate powder in a boiling tube and heat it, you will observe the emission of brown fumes that are of _________________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Nitrogen dioxide.

Key Points

  • Nitrogen dioxide (NO2) is a brown gas that is emitted when lead nitrate is heated.
  • Lead nitrate decomposes to form lead oxide (PbO), nitrogen dioxide (NO2), and oxygen (O2).
  • The chemical reaction for this process is:
    2Pb(NO3)2 → 2PbO + 4NO2 + O2.
  • The brown fumes observed during the heating of lead nitrate are characteristic of nitrogen dioxide.

Additional Information

  • Lead Nitrate (Pb(NO3)2):
    • It is an inorganic compound with the chemical formula Pb(NO3)2.
    • It is soluble in water and is commonly used in laboratories and industries.
    • When heated, lead nitrate decomposes into lead oxide, nitrogen dioxide, and oxygen.
  • Nitrogen Dioxide (NO2):
    • It is a reddish-brown gas with a characteristic sharp, biting odor.
    • It is one of several nitrogen oxides and is a significant air pollutant.
    • NO2 is a major component of smog and can have harmful effects on the respiratory system.
  • Chemical Reactions:
    • In chemistry, a chemical reaction is a process that leads to the transformation of one set of chemical substances to another.
    • Reactions involve the breaking of bonds in reactants and the formation of new bonds in products.
    • Decomposition reactions, like the heating of lead nitrate, involve the breakdown of a single compound into two or more simpler substances.

questions.question: Which is the weakest intermolecular force, considered as the Van der Waals force, often found in halogens, noble gases and other non-polar molecules?
questions.questionHtml: Which is the weakest intermolecular force, considered as the Van der Waals force, often found in halogens, noble gases and other non-polar molecules?
questions.solution: London dispersion forces are the weakest intermolecular forces and a type of Van der Waals force. They are present in all atoms and molecules but are most significant in non-polar molecules, such as halogens and noble gases. These forces arise from temporary fluctuations in electron density, creating instantaneous dipoles that induce dipoles in neighboring molecules, leading to attraction. In contrast, ion-dipole forces, dipole-dipole forces, and dipole-induced dipole forces are stronger. London dispersion forces significantly influence the physical properties of non-polar substances, including their boiling and melting points.

questions.question: ______ states that for a solution of volatile liquids, the partial vapour pressure of each component of the solution is directly proportional to its mole fraction present in solution.
questions.questionHtml: ______ states that for a solution of volatile liquids, the partial vapour pressure of each component of the solution is directly proportional to its mole fraction present in solution.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Raoult’s law.

Raoult’s law states that a solvent’s partial vapour pressure in a solution (or mixture) is equal or identical to the vapour pressure of the pure solvent multiplied by its mole fraction in the solution.

Mathematically, Raoult’s law equation is written as;

Psolution = ΧsolventP0solvent

Where,

Psolution = vapour pressure of the solution
Χsolvent  = mole fraction of the solvent
P0solvent = vapour pressure of the pure solvent

Important Points

Boyle’s law
  • Boyle’s law, also called Mariotte’s law, a relation concerning the compression and expansion of a gas at a constant temperature.
  • The pressure exerted by a gas (of a given mass, kept at a constant temperature) is inversely proportional to the volume occupied by it.
  • The pressure (P) of a given quantity of gas varies inversely with its volume (V) at constant temperature; i.e., in equation form, PV = k, a constant.
Dalton’s law
  • The Law of Partial Pressures, states that the total pressure exerted by a mixture of gases is equal to the sum of the partial pressures of the gases in the mixture.
Faraday’s law
  • Faraday's law of induction (Faraday's law) is a basic law of electromagnetism predicting how a magnetic field will interact with an electric circuit to produce an electromotive force (EMF) - a phenomenon known as electromagnetic induction.

questions.solution: The question identifies a molecular compound from given options. CO<sub>2</sub> is a molecular compound formed by covalent bonding between carbon and oxygen, both nonmetals.
